questions.question: What are the three core concepts that IAM manages for every AWS API call?

options.text: Authentication, Encryption, Audibility
Authentication, Authorization, Audibility
Authentication, Authorization, Availability
Identification, Authorization, Audibility

explanation.correct: IAM handles Authentication (who is making the call), Authorization (is this caller permitted), and Audibility (who did what when, via CloudTrail).
explanation.why: Encryption is handled by KMS/TLS, not IAM. Availability is an infrastructure concern.

questions.question: Which AWS service is responsible for the Audibility pillar of IAM?

options.text: AWS Config
AWS GuardDuty
AWS CloudTrail
AWS Security Hub

explanation.correct: AWS CloudTrail logs every API call with the calling identity, source IP, timestamp, and request parameters — providing the audit record.
explanation.why: Config tracks resource configuration changes. GuardDuty is a threat detection service. Security Hub aggregates findings.

questions.question: How many principal types does IAM recognize?

options.text: Three: root user, IAM user, IAM role
Two: IAM user, IAM role
Four: root user, IAM user, IAM group, IAM role
Five: root user, IAM user, IAM group, IAM role, IAM policy

explanation.correct: IAM recognizes four principal types: root user (account creator, unconstrained), IAM user (long-lived identity), IAM group (permission container, NOT an identity), and IAM role (temporary identity via STS).
explanation.why: IAM policy is not a principal type — it defines permissions but is not an identity that makes API calls.

questions.question: Which IAM principal type is described as 'a costume you put on, do your work, then take off'?

options.text: IAM User
IAM Group
Root User
IAM Role

explanation.correct: IAM roles are temporary identities assumed via AWS STS. They issue short-lived credentials, just like putting on a costume temporarily.
explanation.why: IAM users are long-lived. Groups are containers. Root user is permanent and unconstrained.

questions.question: A company has 50 data engineers who all need the same S3 read permissions. What is the most operationally efficient IAM approach?

options.text: Attach the S3 read policy directly to each of the 50 IAM users
Create one IAM group with the policy attached, add all 50 users to the group
Create one shared IAM user and have all 50 engineers sign in with those credentials
Create one IAM role and have engineers assume it each time they need access

explanation.correct: A group-based model attaches the policy once at the group level. Adding/removing users requires no policy changes. This reduces policy attachment count by ~80%.
explanation.why: Direct user attachment means 50 separate policy edits for any permission change. Shared IAM user destroys auditability. Roles require assumption each time and are better for workloads.

questions.question: Which statement about IAM groups is CORRECT?

options.text: IAM groups can be principals in S3 bucket policies
IAM groups can make API calls directly
IAM groups are permission management containers, not identities
IAM groups are temporary identities issued by STS

explanation.correct: IAM groups are containers for permissions and users — they are NOT identities. Groups cannot make API calls. Only the users inside the group can.
explanation.why: Groups cannot be named as principals in resource-based policies. This is a common exam trap — bucket policies must reference users or roles, not groups.

questions.question: For which tasks is it appropriate to use the AWS root user?

options.text: Daily administrative work including configuring services and deploying resources
Closing the account, changing root email/password, restoring IAM access if locked out
Any task that requires administrator-level permissions
Creating IAM users and groups for the first time

explanation.correct: Root use should be limited to: closing the account, changing root email or password, restoring IAM permissions if revoked, activating IAM billing access, registering as Marketplace seller, enabling GovCloud regions.
explanation.why: Any scenario proposing regular root use is almost always wrong. Daily admin work should use an IAM user or IAM Identity Center federated identity.

questions.question: What does the Action element in an IAM policy specify?

options.text: The AWS resource the policy applies to
Whether the policy allows or denies
One or more API calls in service:operation format
The IAM principal the policy is attached to

explanation.correct: The Action element specifies one or more API calls in service:operation format, such as s3:GetObject, ec2:RunInstances, kms:Decrypt.
explanation.why: A is the Resource element. B is the Effect element. D is the Principal element (only in resource-based policies).

questions.question: Which element is ONLY found in resource-based policies, not identity-based policies?

options.text: Effect
Action
Resource
Principal

explanation.correct: The Principal element is explicit in resource-based policies because the policy lives on the resource and must name who is allowed. In identity-based policies, the principal is implicit (the policy is attached to the identity).
explanation.why: Effect, Action, and Resource are present in both policy types.

questions.question: What does 'implicit deny' mean in AWS IAM?

options.text: A Deny statement that is hidden in a policy
AWS denies access by default when no explicit Allow applies
A Deny that is inherited from a parent OU
A Deny applied automatically when MFA is not present

explanation.correct: AWS is deny-by-default. If no explicit Allow applies (and no explicit Deny is needed), the request is denied automatically. The absence of a permission means no permission.
explanation.why: An implicit deny is the default behavior — not a hidden policy statement. It requires no configuration.

questions.question: Which ARN format is unique to Amazon S3 compared to all other AWS services?

options.text: S3 ARNs do not include the account ID or region
S3 ARNs do not include the service name
S3 ARNs use a different prefix (s3n:// instead of arn:aws:)
S3 ARNs include the VPC ID instead of the account ID

explanation.correct: S3 is the only AWS service where the region and account ID are omitted from the ARN. Format: arn:aws:s3:::bucket-name. This is because S3 bucket names are globally unique.
explanation.why: All other services include region and account ID in their ARNs. This S3-specific format is directly tested on the SAA-C03 exam.

questions.question: What is the correct S3 ARN for all objects in the 'quarterly' prefix of the 'acme-reports' bucket?

options.text: arn:aws:s3:us-east-1:123456789012:acme-reports/quarterly/*
arn:aws:s3:::acme-reports
arn:aws:s3:::acme-reports/quarterly/*
arn:aws:s3:::acme-reports/*

explanation.correct: S3 ARNs have no region and no account ID. The format for objects under a prefix is: arn:aws:s3:::bucket-name/prefix/*.
explanation.why: A incorrectly includes region and account ID. B is the bucket-level ARN (no objects). D covers ALL objects in the bucket, not just the quarterly prefix.

questions.question: A startup founder opens a new AWS account. AWS Trusted Advisor is flagging the account for a security issue. What is the most likely issue?

options.text: No VPC has been created yet
The root user is being used for daily administrative work
No S3 buckets have been created
CloudTrail is not enabled in all regions

explanation.correct: AWS Trusted Advisor flags daily root user use as a high-priority finding. The root user should be locked away after initial setup and an IAM user or Identity Center identity used for daily work.
explanation.why: While CloudTrail configuration is important, the most common Trusted Advisor flag about IAM specifically is root user usage.

questions.question: When an exam scenario mentions 'corporate Active Directory', 'SAML federation', or 'single sign-on across multiple AWS accounts', which AWS service is the correct answer?

options.text: AWS IAM (direct user creation)
AWS Cognito
AWS IAM Identity Center
AWS Directory Service

explanation.correct: IAM Identity Center is AWS's preferred solution for workforce identity management, supporting SAML federation from external IdPs (AD, Okta, Google) and providing SSO across multiple AWS accounts.
explanation.why: Direct IAM user creation doesn't support SSO. Cognito is for app users. Directory Service is a managed directory, not an SSO solution by itself.

questions.question: Which IAM policy element is OPTIONAL?

options.text: Effect
Action
Resource
Condition

explanation.correct: The Condition element is optional. Effect, Action, and Resource are mandatory elements in every IAM policy statement.
explanation.why: Without Effect, Action, and Resource, the policy has no meaning. Condition is only needed when you want to apply contextual constraints.

questions.question: The three-step IAM evaluation rule states that an explicit Deny overrides which of the following?

options.text: Only identity-based policy allows
Only resource-based policy allows
Any Allow in any policy type, same account or cross-account
Any Allow except those granted by service control policies

explanation.correct: The explicit deny rule is invariant. An explicit Deny overrides any Allow anywhere — identity-based, resource-based, permission boundaries, SCPs, session policies — same account or cross-account, without exception.
explanation.why: The rule applies universally. There is no Allow that can override an explicit Deny.

questions.question: A developer's IAM role has an identity-based policy that explicitly allows s3:GetObject. The bucket has a resource-based policy that explicitly denies s3:GetObject for the developer's role. What happens when the developer calls GetObject?

options.text: The call succeeds because identity-based policies and resource-based policies are evaluated independently
The call succeeds because the identity-based policy takes precedence over the bucket policy
The call is denied because the bucket policy explicit Deny overrides the identity-based Allow
The call succeeds because the developer and bucket are in the same account

explanation.correct: The bucket policy's explicit Deny overrides any Allow anywhere. Step 1 of the evaluation rule: is there an explicit Deny? Yes. Deny — evaluation stops. The identity-based Allow is irrelevant.
explanation.why: Identity-based and resource-based policies are not evaluated independently in the sense that a Deny in one cannot be overridden by an Allow in the other.

questions.question: Which action scope grade represents the MOST privileged policy action?

options.text: s3:GetObject
s3:Get*
s3:GetObject and s3:PutObject

explanation.correct: s3:* is wide — it grants every S3 action including GetObject, PutObject, DeleteObject, DeleteBucket, PutBucketPolicy, and PutBucketAcl. This is maximum blast radius.
explanation.why: s3:GetObject is narrow (specific read API). s3:Get* is medium (all read actions). A policy granting exactly GetObject and PutObject is narrower than a wildcard.

questions.question: An application reads S3 object content and lists the bucket to discover keys. Which actions should the policy include?

options.text: s3:* on the bucket ARN
s3:GetObject on object ARN and s3:ListBucket on bucket ARN
s3:GetObject on the bucket ARN only
s3:GetObject and s3:ListObjects on the object ARN

explanation.correct: GetObject is an object-level action requiring the object ARN (bucket/prefix/*). ListBucket is a bucket-level action requiring the bucket ARN. Both are needed and each must target the correct ARN type.
explanation.why: s3:* is too wide. GetObject alone cannot list bucket contents. GetObject on the bucket ARN is incorrect — that ARN type doesn't match the object-level action.

questions.question: What does the 'aws:MultiFactorAuthAge' condition key measure?

options.text: Whether MFA was configured on the IAM user account
The number of MFA devices registered to the user
The number of seconds elapsed since the MFA credential was last issued
Whether MFA was used at any point during the current session

explanation.correct: aws:MultiFactorAuthAge returns the elapsed time in seconds since the MFA credential was issued. Use NumericLessThan: 900 to require MFA within the last 15 minutes.
explanation.why: Option D describes aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent (boolean). Age is a numeric value that increases throughout the session.

questions.question: Which condition protects against session hijacking for destructive S3 actions?

options.text: Condition: Bool: aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent: true
Condition: NumericLessThan: aws:MultiFactorAuthAge: 900
Condition: Bool: aws:SecureTransport: true
Condition: StringEquals: aws:RequestedRegion: us-east-1

explanation.correct: aws:MultiFactorAuthAge with NumericLessThan: 900 requires MFA to have been issued within the last 15 minutes. A hijacked session more than 15 minutes old would fail this check.
explanation.why: MultiFactorAuthPresent is true for the entire session lifetime — a hijacked session retains this value. SecureTransport enforces HTTPS. RequestedRegion restricts to a region.

questions.question: In a cross-account access scenario, Account B's EC2 needs to access S3 in Account A. Which account is the SOURCE account?

options.text: Account A — because it holds the S3 resource
Account B — because that is where the request originates
Both accounts are source accounts
The source account is determined by which account created the IAM role

explanation.correct: The source account is the one MAKING the call — where the request originates. Account B's EC2 initiates the cross-account call. Account A is the destination (the resource owner).
explanation.why: This distinction matters for debugging: the principal's IAM policy is checked in the source account; the role trust policy, bucket policy, and KMS key policy are in the destination account.

questions.question: When does AWS require an explicit Allow on BOTH sides of a cross-account access request?

options.text: Only when the resource is encrypted with KMS
Whenever the principal and resource are in different AWS accounts
Only when using STS AssumeRole
Only when the resource is an S3 bucket

explanation.correct: When the principal and resource are in different AWS accounts, AWS requires an explicit Allow on both sides — the source account must allow the caller to assume the role, and the destination account must have a role trust policy allowing the source.
explanation.why: The two-sided requirement applies to all cross-account access, not just KMS or STS. KMS adds an additional layer with its own key policy.

questions.question: A media company stores customer uploaded videos in Account A encrypted with a customer-managed KMS key. An EC2 workload in Account B needs to read and process these videos. The security team requires no long-lived credentials on the EC2 instances. Which solution is correct?

options.text: Create an IAM user in Account A, store the access keys in AWS Secrets Manager, and configure EC2 instances to retrieve them at runtime

Create an IAM role in Account A with a trust policy for Account B, attach a policy granting s3:GetObject and kms:Decrypt, update the KMS key policy to allow the role, and attach an instance profile to EC2 in Account B to assume the role via STS
Set up AWS PrivateLink with an S3 interface VPC endpoint between Account A and Account B
Configure S3 cross-region replication to copy the videos to a bucket in Account B

explanation.correct: This is the correct cross-account pattern: IAM role in the destination account, trust policy allowing the source account, instance profile with AssumeRole permission, STS issues temporary credentials. The KMS key policy must also be updated (two-pronged rule).
explanation.why: A still uses long-lived credentials (Secrets Manager stores but doesn't eliminate them). C solves a network problem, not an access control problem. D is a data durability feature, not access control.

questions.question: Which two IAM mechanisms would you combine to satisfy these requirements: (1) data analysts can only read S3 data, and (2) developers who temporarily assume the data analyst role cannot gain more than developer-scope permissions?

options.text: Identity-based policy + service control policy
Resource-based bucket policy + IAM group
Identity-based policy with condition + permission boundary on developers
IAM role trust policy + MFA condition

explanation.correct: Identity-based policy on the DataAnalystRole grants s3:GetObject with MFA condition (requirement 1). Permission boundary on developer users caps their maximum effective permissions so assuming the DataAnalystRole cannot extend beyond developer-scope (requirement 4).
explanation.why: Requirement 4 is specifically about preventing developers from gaining extra permissions via role assumption — permission boundaries are the mechanism for capping maximum permissions.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a 'resource-based policy' rather than an 'identity-based policy'?

options.text: A policy attached to an IAM role granting lambda:InvokeFunction
A policy attached to an IAM group granting ec2:DescribeInstances
An S3 bucket policy that allows a specific IAM role to call s3:GetObject
A managed policy granting AdministratorAccess attached to an IAM user

explanation.correct: An S3 bucket policy is attached to the S3 resource (the bucket), not to an IAM identity. It requires an explicit Principal element. This is a resource-based policy.
explanation.why: Policies attached to roles, groups, or users are identity-based. Managed policies are identity-based regardless of what they grant.

questions.question: What is a permission boundary in IAM?

options.text: The maximum number of policies that can be attached to an IAM user
An AWS-managed policy that prevents all IAM changes
A managed policy that caps the maximum effective permissions an IAM user or role can have
A resource-based policy that denies access to specific S3 prefixes

explanation.correct: A permission boundary is a managed policy used as a ceiling — it caps the maximum permissions. The effective permissions of a principal are the intersection of the attached policies and the boundary. Even if a policy grants more, the boundary limits what's actually allowed.
explanation.why: Permission boundaries are often used when developers write their own policies — the boundary ensures they cannot grant themselves admin-level permissions.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of the IAM evaluation rule 'explicit deny wins'?

options.text: To allow resource owners to block access even when identity-based policies grant it
To give SCPs higher priority than bucket policies
To prevent denial of service attacks on IAM
To ensure root users can always override security controls

explanation.correct: The explicit deny rule allows any policy type (especially resource-based policies) to enforce absolute prohibitions that no identity-based Allow can override. This is how security teams enforce 'no public access' or 'no deletion' without touching every individual user policy.
explanation.why: SCPs, bucket policies, permission boundaries all use explicit deny to enforce guardrails regardless of what identity-based policies grant.

questions.question: Which of the following IAM policy structures is MOST aligned with the principle of least privilege?

options.text: Effect: Allow, Action: s3:*, Resource: arn:aws:s3:::acme-reports
Effect: Allow, Action: s3:GetObject, Resource: *
Effect: Allow, Action: s3:GetObject, Resource: arn:aws:s3:::acme-reports/quarterly/*
Effect: Allow, Action: s3:Get*, Resource: arn:aws:s3:::acme-reports/*

explanation.correct: Option C is narrow on both axes: specific action (s3:GetObject only) and specific resource (exactly one prefix in one bucket). This is the ideal least-privilege policy.
explanation.why: A has wide action (s3:*). B has wide resource (*). D has medium action (s3:Get*) and medium resource (all objects in the bucket). C is the only option that is narrow on both axes.

questions.question: An IAM role in Account A has a trust policy that allows Account B to assume it. What does this trust policy enable?

options.text: Account B can use all resources in Account A
Principals in Account B can call sts:AssumeRole to obtain temporary credentials for the role
Account B is merged into Account A for billing purposes
Account B's root user can assume administrator access in Account A

explanation.correct: A trust policy on a role defines who can assume it. Allowing Account B means principals in Account B (who have sts:AssumeRole permission on the role ARN) can call AssumeRole via STS and receive temporary credentials.
explanation.why: Trust policy = who can assume the role. Role policy = what the role can do. The trust policy enables assumption, not full account access.

questions.question: What happens to a cross-account API call after the source account's EC2 instance successfully assumes a role in the destination account?

options.text: IAM continues to treat the call as cross-account for all subsequent policy evaluations
IAM treats the call as a same-account call from the assumed role identity in the destination account
The cross-account session expires after exactly 1 minute
All subsequent calls must go through STS again for each API request

explanation.correct: Once the role is assumed, the caller IS the role in the destination account. IAM treats all subsequent calls as same-account, originating from the assumed role identity. The source account identity is no longer relevant for policy evaluation.
explanation.why: This is why the debugging workflow changes: after assumption, you check the role's policies (destination account), not the EC2's policies (source account).

questions.question: Which MFA mechanism was deprecated by AWS in 2019 and can no longer have new configurations created?

options.text: Virtual MFA (TOTP app)
Hardware MFA (physical token device)
FIDO Security Key
SMS MFA

explanation.correct: SMS MFA was deprecated by AWS in 2019 because it is vulnerable to SIM swapping attacks. Existing configurations remain functional but new ones cannot be created. AWS recommends virtual MFA or FIDO security keys.
explanation.why: Virtual MFA, hardware MFA, and FIDO security keys are all currently supported and recommended.

questions.question: A security architect wants to ensure that S3 deletion of production resources requires MFA, and that a user cannot bypass this by using a session token from a session established with MFA 6 hours ago. Which condition key should be used?

options.text: aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent: true
aws:MultiFactorAuthAge: 21600 (NumericGreaterThan)
aws:MultiFactorAuthAge: 900 (NumericLessThan)
aws:SecureTransport: true

explanation.correct: aws:MultiFactorAuthAge with NumericLessThan: 900 requires MFA to have been issued within the last 15 minutes. A 6-hour-old session would have Age > 900 and the condition would fail, forcing re-authentication.
explanation.why: MultiFactorAuthPresent stays true for the entire session — a 6-hour-old session would still pass. The Age condition with a small threshold is the only way to enforce recency.

questions.question: When debugging a cross-account call to a KMS-encrypted S3 bucket that fails with Access Denied, in what order should you check the four relevant policies?

options.text: KMS key policy → Bucket policy → Role trust policy → Principal's IAM policy
Principal's IAM policy in source account → Role trust policy in destination → Bucket policy in destination → KMS key policy in destination
Bucket policy → Principal's IAM policy → KMS key policy → Role trust policy
Role trust policy → Principal's IAM policy → Bucket policy → KMS key policy

explanation.correct: Check in source-to-destination order: (1) Does the source account principal have sts:AssumeRole? (2) Does the destination role's trust policy allow the source? (3) Does the destination bucket policy permit the action? (4) Does the KMS key policy allow kms:Decrypt for the role?
explanation.why: This is the logical flow of the call: from source account to role assumption to resource access to decryption. Checking in this order quickly identifies where the chain breaks.

questions.question: An application reads S3 object content and receives exact object keys from an SQS queue. It NEVER needs to list bucket contents. Which policy is correct?

options.text: Effect: Allow, Action: [s3:GetObject, s3:ListBucket], Resource: [bucket-arn, bucket-arn/*]
Effect: Allow, Action: s3:GetObject, Resource: arn:aws:s3:::acme-reports/quarterly/*
Effect: Allow, Action: s3:*, Resource: arn:aws:s3:::acme-reports/*
Effect: Allow, Action: s3:GetObject, Resource: *

explanation.correct: Since the application receives exact keys and never enumerates the bucket, only s3:GetObject is needed on the specific prefix ARN. Adding ListBucket would violate least privilege.
explanation.why: A adds ListBucket which the question explicitly says is not needed. C uses s3:* which is too wide. D uses * resource which is too wide.

questions.question: What is the KMS two-pronged authorization rule for cross-account decryption?

options.text: Both the bucket policy and the IAM role policy must allow kms:Decrypt
Both the IAM role policy and the KMS key resource policy must independently permit kms:Decrypt
Both the source account SCP and the destination account IAM policy must allow kms:Decrypt
The KMS key policy alone is sufficient for cross-account decryption

explanation.correct: KMS uses two-pronged authorization: the IAM role policy must allow kms:Decrypt AND the KMS key resource policy must independently allow kms:Decrypt for that role. Missing either one causes Access Denied.
explanation.why: The KMS key policy alone is not sufficient — the caller's IAM role must also have the permission. This double-check is unique to KMS and is tested directly on the SAA-C03.

questions.question: What is the correct description of how AWS IAM evaluates policies?

options.text: The most permissive policy wins — if any Allow exists, access is granted
Identity-based policies are evaluated before resource-based policies
Explicit deny wins; explicit allow grants; implicit deny is the default
Resource-based policies always override identity-based policies

explanation.correct: The three-step rule: (1) explicit deny anywhere → deny, stop. (2) explicit allow → allow. (3) neither → implicit deny by default. This rule applies to all policy types equally.
explanation.why: There is no most-permissive-wins rule in IAM. There is no ordering between policy types — all are evaluated simultaneously. Resource-based policies do not override identity-based.

questions.question: Which of the following is a valid use case for an IAM role rather than an IAM user?

options.text: A human engineer who needs daily access to the AWS Console
An EC2 instance that needs to write logs to CloudWatch
A team of developers who all need the same S3 read access
An administrator who needs MFA-protected access to billing

explanation.correct: Workloads (EC2, Lambda, ECS, EKS, Fargate) should always use IAM roles — the instance profile provides temporary credentials automatically. Roles avoid long-lived access keys on instances.
explanation.why: Humans use IAM users or federated identities. Teams use IAM groups. Roles are for workloads and cross-account patterns.

questions.question: A regulated company requires that IAM policies granting deletion permissions on production resources must be audited. A security engineer grades each policy on a two-axis rubric. Which policy would be REJECTED?

options.text: Effect: Allow, Action: s3:DeleteObject, Resource: arn:aws:s3:::prod-bucket/archive/*
Effect: Allow, Action: s3:DeleteObject, Resource: *
Effect: Allow, Action: s3:DeleteObject, Resource: arn:aws:s3:::prod-bucket/*
Effect: Allow, Action: s3:DeleteObject, Resource: arn:aws:s3:::prod-bucket/archive/2024/*

explanation.correct: Option B has a wildcard resource (*) — wide on the resource axis. This means DeleteObject can be called on ANY S3 object in ANY bucket in the account. This is immediately rejected.
explanation.why: A, C, and D all have specific ARN resources (narrow to medium). B's Resource: * is the widest possible scope — rejected without further consideration.

questions.question: What does the instance profile do when attached to an EC2 instance?

options.text: Encrypts the EC2 instance's root volume
Provides the EC2 instance with temporary IAM role credentials via the instance metadata service
Attaches a dedicated VPC security group to the instance
Grants the EC2 instance cross-region access

explanation.correct: An instance profile is a container for an IAM role. When attached to EC2, it provides the instance with automatic access to temporary credentials via the metadata service (169.254.169.254). No long-lived access keys are needed.
explanation.why: Instance profiles are the standard mechanism for giving EC2 instances IAM permissions without embedding access keys in the instance.

questions.question: Which of the following actions would cause an IAM evaluation to fail at Step 1 (Explicit Deny) even though the identity-based policy has an Allow?

options.text: The user has not enabled MFA on their account
A bucket policy contains an explicit Deny for the user's role on s3:GetObject
The user's session has expired
The resource is in a different AWS region

explanation.correct: An explicit Deny in a bucket policy triggers Step 1 of the evaluation rule. The identity-based Allow is evaluated simultaneously but cannot override the explicit Deny — the call is denied immediately.
explanation.why: Absence of MFA, session expiration, and region differences would cause a Condition failure or authentication failure, not an explicit Deny evaluation.

questions.question: A company is migrating from per-user IAM policy attachments to IAM groups. A consultant says this typically reduces the number of policy attachments by 80%. What else does it improve?

options.text: Reduces AWS monthly billing costs
Makes permission changes a single edit at the group level instead of editing each user
Allows IAM groups to be used as principals in S3 bucket policies
Eliminates the need for MFA on individual IAM users

explanation.correct: With group-based policies, changing a permission (e.g., adding access to a new service) is a one-line edit at the group level. Without groups, it would require 40+ edits — one per user. New engineers get permissions just by being added to the group.
explanation.why: Groups do not affect billing. Groups still cannot be S3 bucket policy principals. MFA is still required on individual users.

questions.question: What is the relationship between a permission boundary and an identity-based policy?

options.text: The effective permissions are the UNION of the boundary and the policy
The identity-based policy overrides the boundary
The effective permissions are the INTERSECTION of the boundary and the attached policy
The boundary only applies to cross-account actions

explanation.correct: Effective permissions = intersection of (what the boundary allows) AND (what the policy grants). If a policy grants s3:*, but the boundary only allows s3:GetObject and s3:PutObject, the effective permissions are just GetObject and PutObject.
explanation.why: The boundary acts as a ceiling. The identity-based policy cannot grant more than the boundary allows. Union would mean the boundary has no effect.

questions.question: A company has a compliance requirement: any IAM user who can delete production resources must re-authenticate with MFA within the last 15 minutes before performing deletion. The company already enforces MFA at sign-in. Which approach satisfies this with LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Enable MFA at sign-in for all IAM users — this already satisfies the requirement since every session is MFA-backed
Add aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent: true condition to deletion policies
Add aws:MultiFactorAuthAge: 900 (NumericLessThan) condition to deletion policies
Move all production resources to a separate account and configure IAM Identity Center to require MFA for role assumption into that account

explanation.correct: MultiFactorAuthAge: 900 with NumericLessThan requires a fresh MFA credential — meaning the user must re-authenticate within the last 15 minutes before deletion. This is enforced per-action with no additional infrastructure.
explanation.why: A and B both fail because MultiFactorAuthPresent stays true for the entire session — a hijacked 8-hour-old session would still pass. D adds significant overhead and architectural complexity.

questions.question: A security team wants to prevent all principals in an AWS organization from disabling CloudTrail, including account administrators with AdministratorAccess. Which mechanism achieves this?

options.text: A resource-based policy on the CloudTrail trail
A permission boundary on all admin IAM users
An SCP at the root of the organization denying cloudtrail:StopLogging and cloudtrail:DeleteTrail
An IAM identity-based policy denying CloudTrail actions on all admin users

explanation.correct: Service Control Policies (SCPs) at the AWS Organizations root level apply to all principals in all member accounts — including those with AdministratorAccess. An SCP explicit deny cannot be overridden by any identity-based Allow.
explanation.why: Resource-based policies on a trail can be bypassed by an admin. Permission boundaries require manual application to each user. Identity-based denies are per-user and can be removed by an admin.

questions.question: Which combination of IAM policies satisfies ALL of these requirements: analysts can read data, analysts can never delete data, reads require fresh MFA (within 15 min), developers assuming the analyst role cannot gain additional permissions?

options.text: Identity-based policy on analyst role with s3:GetObject + MFA age condition; SCP denying s3:Delete for the entire account

Identity-based policy on analyst role granting s3:GetObject with MultiFactorAuthAge: 900 condition; resource-based bucket policy with explicit Deny on s3:DeleteObject for the analyst role; permission boundary on developer users
IAM managed policy granting s3:GetObject and explicitly denying s3:DeleteObject; MFA required at sign-in
Resource-based bucket policy granting s3:GetObject with MFA condition; IAM group-based policy denying delete

explanation.correct: B uses three mechanisms correctly: (1) Identity-based policy on analyst role with MultiFactorAuthAge: 900 satisfies read-only + fresh MFA. (2) Bucket policy explicit Deny on Delete satisfies absolute no-deletion. (3) Permission boundary on developers satisfies the no-escalation requirement.
explanation.why: A uses an SCP for delete prevention which is organization-wide overkill and doesn't prevent escalation. C lacks fresh MFA enforcement (sign-in MFA is session-wide). D doesn't address developer escalation.

questions.question: What is the correct IAM principal selection when a scenario asks how to provide a Lambda function with access to DynamoDB?

options.text: IAM user with access keys embedded in the Lambda environment variables
IAM group with DynamoDB policy, Lambda as a member
IAM role with DynamoDB permissions attached to the Lambda execution role
IAM policy with Principal: Lambda directly

explanation.correct: Workloads (Lambda, EC2, ECS, Fargate) should use IAM roles. Lambda has an execution role — the Lambda service assumes this role when running the function. Temporary credentials are provided automatically.
explanation.why: Embedding access keys in Lambda environment variables creates long-lived credential exposure risk. Groups cannot be Lambda's execution role. You cannot attach a policy with Principal: Lambda directly — roles use trust policies.

questions.question: A developer notices that their new production S3 bucket was accidentally deleted. The post-incident review shows that the developer's IAM role had a policy including s3:DeleteBucket on resource: *. The developer says 'but I just meant to grant full control over our app bucket.' What is the correct fix?

options.text: Remove s3:DeleteBucket from the policy entirely — developers should never have delete permissions
Replace s3:* with a list of the specific APIs the application actually uses, scoped to the specific bucket ARN
Add a Condition: StringEquals: s3:prefix: app-bucket to restrict the wildcard
Change the resource from * to arn:aws:s3:::app-bucket to narrow the resource scope

explanation.correct: The fix should address BOTH axes: narrow the action scope to only the APIs actually needed AND narrow the resource to the specific bucket ARN. Resource narrowing alone (D) still allows s3:DeleteBucket on that one bucket. Removing delete entirely (A) may be too restrictive.
explanation.why: The two-axis grading rubric requires narrowing both action and resource. s3:DeleteBucket on a specific bucket ARN is still dangerous if delete wasn't intended. The correct fix is to list only the needed APIs.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes a real-world production use case for a resource-based bucket policy's explicit Deny?

options.text: Granting read access to an S3 bucket across multiple IAM users
Blocking S3 public access without modifying every individual user policy
Allowing EC2 to write logs to an S3 bucket
Encrypting all objects stored in an S3 bucket

explanation.correct: A resource-based bucket policy with an explicit Deny on s3:GetObject for Principal: * blocks public access to everyone — even principals whose identity-based policies would grant access. This is how security teams enforce 'no public access' without touching each user's policies.
explanation.why: Granting access to multiple users is an identity-based pattern. EC2 log writes use an IAM role. Encryption is S3 default encryption or KMS, not an IAM policy.

questions.question: A company wants to grant its 30 AWS accounts' engineers single sign-on with their corporate Active Directory, enforce MFA at sign-in, and use role-based access with defined permission sets per job function. Which AWS service and architecture achieves this?

options.text: Create IAM users in each of the 30 accounts with SAML assertions
AWS IAM Identity Center federated from the corporate Active Directory, with permission sets assigned to accounts in AWS Organizations
AWS Cognito User Pools with Active Directory integration
Per-account IAM roles with SAML trust relationships to the corporate IdP

explanation.correct: IAM Identity Center is the AWS preferred solution for multi-account SSO. It federates from Active Directory via SAML/SCIM, manages permission sets centrally, and assigns them to accounts in AWS Organizations. MFA is enforced via the Identity Center settings.
explanation.why: Per-account IAM users at scale are unmanageable. Cognito is for app user authentication, not workforce. Per-account SAML roles work but require management in each of 30 accounts — IAM Identity Center centralizes this.

questions.question: What information does AWS CloudTrail capture for every API call?

options.text: The IAM policy that was evaluated
The calling identity, source IP, timestamp, and request parameters
The data that was read or written to the AWS resource
The cost associated with the API call

explanation.correct: CloudTrail captures: who made the call (calling identity), where from (source IP), when (timestamp), and what was requested (request parameters/action). This is the audit record for all AWS activity.
explanation.why: CloudTrail does not capture the actual data content (e.g., S3 object contents). It captures metadata about the API call, not billing data.

questions.question: What is an ARN (Amazon Resource Name)?

options.text: An AWS API authentication token
A globally unique address for every resource in AWS
An access right notation used in bucket policies
An AWS region naming convention

explanation.correct: An ARN is the globally unique address of every resource in AWS. Every S3 object, EC2 instance, KMS key, Lambda function, IAM role — all have ARNs. ARNs are used in IAM policies to specify which resource an action applies to.
explanation.why: ARNs are not tokens or region names. They are resource identifiers used throughout AWS.

questions.question: A new AWS account is created. What are the MINIMUM four steps to secure it according to AWS best practices?

options.text: Create 10 IAM users, enable CloudTrail, create an S3 bucket, enable billing alerts
Enable MFA on root, create an IAM admin user, enable MFA on IAM user, store root credentials offline
Delete the root user, enable GuardDuty, create IAM roles, enable VPC Flow Logs
Enable MFA on root, create an IAM admin user, share the root password with all admins, enable CloudTrail

explanation.correct: The four-step root lockdown pattern: (1) Enable MFA on root during initial setup. (2) Create an IAM admin user for daily work. (3) Enable MFA on the IAM admin user. (4) Store root credentials in a secure offline location (physical safe).
explanation.why: You cannot delete the root user. Sharing the root password is the opposite of security. Enabling GuardDuty is useful but not part of the root lockdown pattern.

questions.question: Which element in an IAM policy makes it a 'resource-based policy' rather than an 'identity-based policy'?

options.text: The Effect element set to 'Deny'
The Action element containing resource-level APIs
The explicit Principal element naming an IAM identity
The Condition element containing MFA requirements

explanation.correct: The presence of an explicit Principal element is what makes a policy resource-based. Resource-based policies live on the resource and must name the identity being granted or denied access. Identity-based policies have no Principal element — it's implicit.
explanation.why: Effect, Action, and Condition elements appear in both policy types. Only Principal distinguishes resource-based.

questions.question: An IAM role has NO policies attached. What is the result when a Lambda function with this execution role tries to read an S3 object?

options.text: The call succeeds because Lambda functions have implicit S3 read access
The call fails with Access Denied — implicit deny applies with no policies attached
The call succeeds if the S3 bucket has a bucket policy allowing Lambda
The call succeeds because the bucket is in the same account as the Lambda

explanation.correct: With no policies attached and no resource-based policy granting access, the three-step evaluation reaches Step 3: implicit deny. AWS is deny-by-default. No Allow = no access.
explanation.why: Lambda has no implicit S3 access. Same-account does not mean same permissions. A bucket policy granting access would help, but the question states no policies exist.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the services that support resource-based policies?

options.text: Amazon S3
AWS KMS
Amazon EC2
Amazon SQS

explanation.correct: EC2 does not support resource-based policies. EC2 instances use identity-based policies attached to IAM roles. The 9 services that support resource-based policies are: S3, KMS, SQS, SNS, Lambda, ECR, EFS, API Gateway, Secrets Manager.
explanation.why: S3 (bucket policies), KMS (key policies), and SQS (queue policies) all support resource-based policies. EC2 does not.

questions.question: What is 'federation' in the context of IAM Identity Center?

options.text: Linking two AWS accounts together for billing purposes
Using an external identity provider (Active Directory, Okta) to authenticate users, who then receive temporary AWS credentials
Copying IAM policies from one account to another
Merging multiple IAM roles into a single federated role

explanation.correct: Federation allows users to authenticate with an external identity provider (corporate AD, Google, Okta) via SAML or OIDC. The IdP vouches for the user's identity, and IAM grants temporary credentials. No IAM user needs to be created per person.
explanation.why: Federation is about identity delegation, not billing or policy copying. IAM Identity Center uses federation to provide SSO.

questions.question: In the ACME Media cross-account scenario, why is there no need to store long-lived AWS access keys on the EC2 instances in Account B?

options.text: EC2 instances automatically have read access to all S3 buckets in the same organization
The instance profile attached to the EC2 provides temporary credentials via STS AssumeRole — no static keys needed
S3 buckets grant access to all EC2 instances in the same VPC by default
AWS Organizations automatically shares credentials across accounts

explanation.correct: The instance profile contains a role that permits sts:AssumeRole on the Account A role. STS issues temporary credentials (access key, secret, session token) that expire automatically. The instance metadata service delivers these transparently — no key management required.
explanation.why: EC2 has no default S3 access. VPC-based access requires VPC endpoints and explicit policies. AWS Organizations shares guardrails (SCPs), not credentials.

questions.question: What does an SCP (Service Control Policy) do in AWS Organizations?

options.text: It creates IAM policies automatically for all users in the organization
It sets maximum permission boundaries for all principals in an account or OU — even account root users
It synchronizes IAM policies across all member accounts
It logs all API calls in all member accounts to a central S3 bucket

explanation.correct: SCPs are guardrails applied at the AWS Organizations level. They cap what any principal in the account or OU can do — even the account's root user. An SCP Deny cannot be overridden by any identity-based Allow in the member account.
explanation.why: SCPs do not create or sync IAM policies. CloudTrail handles centralized audit logging. SCPs control maximum permissions, not create policies.

questions.question: An IAM policy has Effect: Allow, Action: s3:GetObject, Resource: arn:aws:s3:::acme-reports. What is wrong with this policy?

options.text: S3 ARNs must include the region
s3:GetObject is an object-level action but the resource is a bucket-level ARN without an object path
The Effect should be Permit, not Allow
S3 resource ARNs must include the account ID

explanation.correct: s3:GetObject is an object-level API that requires an object ARN (arn:aws:s3:::bucket-name/*). The bucket ARN without an object path (arn:aws:s3:::acme-reports) is correct for bucket-level operations like s3:ListBucket. The action and resource type are mismatched.
explanation.why: S3 ARNs correctly omit region and account ID. 'Allow' is the correct value. The mismatch between object-level action and bucket-level ARN is the error.

questions.question: A security engineer reviews a policy and finds: Effect: Allow, Action: [s3:GetObject, s3:ListBucket], Resource: *. How would you grade this policy?

options.text: Narrow on both axes — acceptable for production
Narrow on action, wide on resource — flag for review and tighten resource before production
Wide on both axes — reject immediately
Medium on action, narrow on resource — acceptable with justification

explanation.correct: The action scope is narrow (specific APIs: GetObject and ListBucket). The resource scope is wide (Resource: * = all S3 resources in the account). This is narrow-action, wide-resource. It should be flagged and the resource tightened to the specific bucket before production use.
explanation.why: Two specific APIs = narrow action. Resource: * = wide. Not both wide so not immediately rejected, but not production-ready until resource is narrowed.

questions.question: A company wants its Lambda functions to access DynamoDB tables only in the same region, with no access to tables in other regions. Which IAM mechanism enforces this?

options.text: Attach a VPC security group restricting outbound traffic to the DynamoDB endpoint
Add a Condition: StringEquals: aws:RequestedRegion: us-east-1 to the Lambda execution role's policy
Create an SCP denying DynamoDB access outside us-east-1
Both B and C are valid options depending on whether the restriction is per-function or per-account

explanation.correct: Both are valid: a Condition key in the Lambda's execution role policy restricts that specific Lambda. An SCP at the account or OU level would restrict all functions in the account. The right choice depends on scope — per-function or per-account guardrail.
explanation.why: VPC security groups control network traffic, not IAM authorization. Either the Condition key (per-role) or SCP (per-account) is appropriate depending on the scope needed.

questions.question: What is an 'anti-pattern' that the IAM lecture specifically calls out as destroying auditability?

options.text: Enabling MFA for all IAM users
Using IAM roles for EC2 workloads instead of access keys
Creating one IAM user per environment (dev-user, staging-user, prod-user) shared across the team
Using IAM groups to manage permissions for teams

explanation.correct: Creating shared IAM users per environment (all developers use 'dev-user') destroys auditability because CloudTrail cannot distinguish which individual developer took which action. The correct pattern is one IAM identity per human with environment access through groups or role assumption.
explanation.why: MFA, IAM roles for workloads, and IAM groups are all best practices — the opposite of anti-patterns.

questions.question: A developer writes an IAM policy with Resource: * to 'just get it working' during development. Why is this dangerous even if the action scope is narrow?

options.text: Resource: * causes higher AWS charges
The policy will apply to resources in all AWS regions
The narrow action on a wide resource scope still violates least privilege, and shortcuts like this are commonly forgotten and deployed to production
Resource: * is invalid syntax in IAM policies

explanation.correct: The lecture specifically calls this out: 'getting things working' shortcuts often never get cleaned up. A narrow action with Resource: * still allows that action on every resource in the account. The real incident described in the lecture (accidentally deleted production bucket) resulted from exactly this pattern.
explanation.why: Resource: * is valid syntax and does not increase billing directly. The risk is blast radius and the human tendency to forget to tighten shortcuts.

questions.question: When writing an S3 bucket policy to allow cross-account access, why can't you use an IAM group as the Principal?

options.text: IAM groups are not supported in the same account
IAM groups are permission management containers and not identities — they cannot make API calls or be named as principals
Cross-account bucket policies require STS principals only
IAM groups require explicit trust policies before they can be used in bucket policies

explanation.correct: Groups are containers, not identities. They have no ARN that can be used as a Principal in a resource-based policy. You must reference the underlying IAM users or roles that belong to the group.
explanation.why: Groups within the same account are perfectly valid in identity-based policies, but cannot be principals in resource-based policies (like bucket policies) regardless of account.

questions.question: A junior engineer asks: 'If I give my IAM user AdministratorAccess, why is that better than just using the root user for everything?' What is the BEST answer?

options.text: IAM users with AdministratorAccess have more permissions than the root user
IAM users can be disabled or have credentials rotated if compromised; root credentials are permanent and cannot be revoked
IAM users have lower AWS service limits than the root user
AdministratorAccess is the same as root — there is no difference

explanation.correct: The critical advantage: if an IAM user is compromised, you can disable it, rotate credentials, or delete it. You cannot 'disable' the root user — it is permanent. Root compromise = account compromise with no easy recovery. IAM users are controllable; root is not.
explanation.why: Root actually has MORE unconstrained permissions than AdministratorAccess (root bypasses SCPs, permission boundaries). The difference is about manageability and recovery, not permissions.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes what happens when a FIDO security key is used for MFA?

options.text: It sends a one-time code via SMS to the user's phone
It generates a time-based OTP using an algorithm on a mobile app
It uses public-key cryptography with a hardware device; the credential is phishing-resistant and bound to the original domain
It stores credentials in a cloud-synced password manager

explanation.correct: FIDO security keys (like Google Titan) use public-key cryptography. The private key never leaves the hardware device. The credential is bound to the original domain and cannot be replayed against a different domain — making it phishing-resistant.
explanation.why: A describes SMS MFA (deprecated). B describes virtual MFA (TOTP app). D describes passkeys (FIDO2 syncable).

questions.question: A Solutions Architect is reviewing IAM policies for an exam question scenario. The policy has: Effect: Allow, Action: s3:GetObject, Resource: arn:aws:s3:::reports, Condition: Bool: aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent: true. What is wrong with this policy?

options.text: s3:GetObject cannot have a Condition element
s3:GetObject is an object-level action but the resource ARN is a bucket-level ARN with no object path
aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent should be False, not True
The ARN is missing the region and account ID

explanation.correct: s3:GetObject operates on objects, requiring an ARN like arn:aws:s3:::reports/* or arn:aws:s3:::reports/prefix/*. The bucket ARN (arn:aws:s3:::reports) is for bucket-level operations like s3:ListBucket. Action-to-ARN type mismatch.
explanation.why: Conditions on s3:GetObject are valid. MultiFactorAuthPresent: true is correct syntax. S3 ARNs correctly omit region and account ID.

questions.question: In an exam scenario question, the answer options include two policies: Policy A has narrow action and wildcard resource. Policy B has wildcard action and narrow resource. Which policy best follows least privilege?

options.text: Policy A — narrow action is more important than narrow resource
Policy B — narrow resource is more important than narrow action
Neither — both are equally bad and both violate least privilege
Policy A is slightly better but only if the resource is encrypted

explanation.correct: The lecture is explicit: 'A wildcard action with a narrow resource is just as bad as a narrow action with a wildcard resource. Audit both scopes independently.' Both policies fail the two-axis grading rubric. The correct answer requires narrow on BOTH axes.
explanation.why: There is no ranking between wide-action-narrow-resource and narrow-action-wide-resource — both are violations. The only correct policy is narrow on both.

questions.question: A company needs to enforce that all S3 bucket policies in every account across their 50-account AWS Organization must deny public access. Which mechanism is MOST efficient?

options.text: Manually add a public access Deny statement to each bucket policy in all 50 accounts
Create a Lambda function that scans all buckets daily and adds Deny statements
Apply an SCP at the AWS Organizations root that denies s3:PutBucketPolicy unless the policy blocks public access, AND enable S3 Block Public Access at the organization level
Use IAM Access Analyzer to monitor public buckets and email administrators

explanation.correct: An SCP at the organization root automatically applies to all accounts — no per-account management. Combining it with S3 Block Public Access at the organization level provides defense in depth. New accounts and new buckets are protected immediately.
explanation.why: Manual bucket policies and Lambda scanning require ongoing maintenance. Access Analyzer monitors but doesn't prevent — it's reactive, not preventive.

questions.question: What role does AWS STS (Security Token Service) play in IAM role assumption?

options.text: STS is a storage service for long-lived IAM credentials
STS issues short-lived temporary credentials (access key, secret key, session token) when a principal calls AssumeRole
STS is the service that evaluates IAM policy evaluation logic
STS manages MFA device registration for IAM users

explanation.correct: AWS STS issues temporary security credentials when AssumeRole is called. These credentials include an access key ID, secret access key, and session token. They expire automatically (typically 1 hour) and do not need rotation — they are self-expiring.
explanation.why: STS doesn't store credentials (it generates them). Policy evaluation is done by IAM. MFA registration is managed in IAM console.

questions.question: A bucket policy says: Effect: Deny, Principal: *, Action: s3:GetObject, Resource: arn:aws:s3:::public-data/*. An IAM role has an identity-based policy that explicitly allows s3:GetObject on the same ARN. What is the result?

options.text: Access granted — identity-based policy overrides bucket policy for same-account principals
Access denied — the bucket policy explicit Deny applies to ALL principals including those with identity-based Allows
Access granted — when both policies exist, the Allow takes precedence
Access depends on which policy was created most recently

explanation.correct: The bucket policy has Effect: Deny for Principal: * (everyone). An explicit Deny overrides any Allow anywhere. Even an identity-based policy Allow for the same principal cannot overcome the bucket policy's explicit Deny. Step 1 of the evaluation rule: explicit Deny found → deny.
explanation.why: No policy ordering or recency matters. The explicit deny rule is absolute and invariant.

questions.question: A cloud engineer says 'the production architecture pattern for MFA is: enforce Present for read-only operations, and use Age for destructive operations.' Why is this the recommended pattern?

options.text: Present is more secure than Age for all operations
Present allows daily reads without re-authentication while Age forces re-authentication for high-risk actions, balancing usability and security
Age cannot be used for read-only operations due to IAM limitations
Present and Age are equivalent for destructive operations

explanation.correct: Users sign in once with MFA at the start of the day — MultiFactorAuthPresent = true for the session, allowing routine reads. Destructive operations require aws:MultiFactorAuthAge: 900 — the user must have authenticated with MFA within the last 15 minutes. This means routine work isn't interrupted but high-risk actions require a fresh MFA challenge.
explanation.why: Present stays true all session — useful for reads. Age forces recency — required for destructive actions to defend against hijacking. They solve different problems.

questions.question: Which IAM construct represents what the lecture calls 'temporary access like assuming a superpower for the day, then going back to normal'?

options.text: IAM User with MFA
IAM Group with time-based conditions
IAM Role assumed via STS
IAM Policy with session duration limit

explanation.correct: IAM roles are described as costumes — you put them on via STS AssumeRole, do your work with those permissions, and the temporary credentials expire automatically. You take off the costume and return to your base identity.
explanation.why: IAM users are permanent identities. IAM groups are containers. IAM policies define permissions but are not temporary identities themselves.

questions.question: What is the MINIMUM IAM policy required for an EC2 instance in Account B to assume a role in Account A?

options.text: AdministratorAccess managed policy
An identity-based policy allowing sts:AssumeRole on the specific role ARN in Account A
A resource-based policy on the EC2 instance
An SCP allowing sts:AssumeRole in Account A

explanation.correct: The instance's IAM role (via instance profile) needs an identity-based policy with Effect: Allow, Action: sts:AssumeRole, Resource: [role ARN in Account A]. This is the minimum — and it follows least privilege by naming the specific role ARN.
explanation.why: AdministratorAccess is far too permissive. EC2 instances don't have resource-based policies. SCPs are organization-level controls, not per-instance permissions.

questions.question: Which of the following would you see in a CloudTrail log entry for a cross-account S3 GetObject call by an assumed role?

options.text: The permanent IAM user ARN of the EC2 instance's operator
The assumed role ARN (DataAnalystRole) with the session name, source IP of the EC2 instance, and the S3 object key accessed
Only the account ID of the source account, not the specific role
The KMS key ARN used for decryption only

explanation.correct: CloudTrail captures: the assumed role identity (arn:aws:sts::accountid:assumed-role/DataAnalystRole/session-name), source IP of the caller, timestamp, and request parameters including the S3 object key. This provides full forensic detail.
explanation.why: After role assumption, the calling identity in CloudTrail is the assumed role, not the original EC2 instance's role or operator. Source account information is available but the role ARN is the primary identity.

questions.question: A company implements 'defense in depth' for its S3 data. Layer 1: identity-based policy with s3:GetObject only. Layer 2: bucket policy explicit Deny on DeleteObject. Layer 3: permission boundaries on developers. Layer 4: CloudTrail data events. What does Layer 4 specifically provide?

options.text: Prevention of unauthorized access
Audit trail and detection capability — forensic evidence even if Layers 1-3 were somehow bypassed
Encryption of all S3 objects at rest
Real-time blocking of malicious API calls

explanation.correct: CloudTrail data events provide detection and forensics — the audit trail. If layers 1-3 fail or are bypassed, CloudTrail provides the record of what happened, when, who did it, and from what source. This enables incident response.
explanation.why: Layers 1-2 provide prevention. Boundaries cap permissions. CloudTrail doesn't prevent or encrypt — it records. Real-time blocking is done by services like GuardDuty + automated remediation.

questions.question: Which four MFA mechanisms does AWS support for IAM users and the root user?

options.text: SMS, Email, Virtual MFA, Hardware MFA
Virtual MFA (TOTP app), Hardware MFA (physical token), FIDO Security Key, Passkey
Virtual MFA, Hardware MFA, Biometric, Passkey
Google Authenticator, Authy, Yubikey, SMS

explanation.correct: AWS supports four MFA mechanisms: Virtual MFA (TOTP apps like Google Authenticator), Hardware MFA (physical token devices), FIDO Security Key (public-key cryptography hardware), and Passkeys (FIDO2 device-bound or syncable). SMS MFA was deprecated in 2019.
explanation.why: Email is not an MFA mechanism. Biometric is part of passkeys but not a standalone mechanism. Naming specific apps (Google Authenticator, Authy, Yubikey) are examples within the categories, not the categories themselves.

questions.question: A developer has a policy that grants s3:PutObject on a production S3 bucket. A bucket policy explicitly denies s3:PutObject for ALL principals. The developer's identity-based policy does NOT include a Deny. What is the result?

options.text: The PutObject call succeeds because the identity-based Allow is present
The PutObject call is denied because the bucket policy explicit Deny overrides all Allows
The result depends on which policy was applied more recently
The result depends on whether the developer is in the same account as the bucket

explanation.correct: The bucket policy explicit Deny for all principals (*) triggers Step 1 of the evaluation rule. The developer's identity-based Allow is irrelevant — the explicit Deny wins. This is true whether the developer and bucket are in the same account or different accounts.
explanation.why: Policy recency does not affect evaluation. Same-account or cross-account doesn't change the explicit deny rule. The only thing that matters is the presence of an explicit Deny.

questions.question: What is the 'blast radius' concept in IAM security?

options.text: The geographic region affected by an AWS outage
The maximum damage that could be done if a given IAM identity or credential is compromised
The number of API calls an IAM policy allows per second
The cost impact of misconfigured IAM policies on the AWS bill

explanation.correct: Blast radius in IAM security refers to the maximum damage scope if a credential or identity is compromised. A root user with wildcard permissions has maximum blast radius (entire account). An application role with s3:GetObject on one prefix has minimal blast radius. Least privilege minimizes blast radius.
explanation.why: This is an IAM security concept, not related to geographic availability, API rate limits, or billing.

questions.question: A company audit finds an IAM policy with: Effect: Allow, Action: s3:*, Resource: arn:aws:s3:::sensitive-data-bucket/*. The developer's intent was to give 'full control of our app bucket.' What specific risks exist in this policy?

options.text: s3:* includes s3:DeleteBucket which could delete the bucket, and s3:PutBucketPolicy which could modify access controls
The policy is too narrow — it should use Resource: * for full bucket control
The policy is correct — s3:* on a specific bucket ARN is always acceptable
The only risk is that s3:* costs more than specific API grants

explanation.correct: s3:* includes dangerous admin-level actions: s3:DeleteBucket (delete the entire bucket), s3:PutBucketPolicy (change who has access), s3:PutBucketAcl (change bucket permissions), s3:DeleteObject (delete any object). None of these were likely intended for an application role. Tightening to the specific APIs used has zero functional impact and removes significant risk.
explanation.why: The resource scope is appropriately narrow (specific bucket). The problem is the action scope (wildcard). The fix is to list only the APIs the application actually calls.

questions.question: A security team needs to give data scientists read access to an S3 data lake while ensuring they cannot access PII objects stored in a /pii/ prefix. Which combination of policies achieves this with least privilege?

options.text: Grant s3:GetObject on the entire bucket and rely on data scientists' professionalism
Grant s3:GetObject on bucket/data/* with an explicit Deny on bucket/pii/* using a bucket policy
Grant s3:GetObject on bucket/* and enable CloudTrail to detect PII access
Use IAM Access Analyzer to detect when PII is accessed

explanation.correct: Two-layer approach: identity-based policy grants GetObject on the data/* prefix only (narrow resource), AND a bucket policy explicit Deny on the pii/* prefix ensures no matter what identity-based policies are attached, PII access is absolutely blocked.
explanation.why: Relying on professionalism is not a security control. CloudTrail detects but doesn't prevent. Access Analyzer is auditing, not prevention. Explicit Deny + narrow Allow is the right combination.

questions.question: In the IAM policy anatomy, what does the Condition element's key-value pair represent?

options.text: The list of AWS services the policy applies to
A contextual test that constrains when the policy applies — based on request context like source IP, MFA status, time of day
The encryption algorithm used for the policy document
The IAM user attributes required to apply the policy

explanation.correct: The Condition element contains key-value tests based on request context. Examples: aws:SourceIp (caller's IP), aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent (boolean), aws:MultiFactorAuthAge (seconds), aws:RequestedRegion, aws:CurrentTime. These constrain WHEN the policy applies without changing WHAT it grants.
explanation.why: Conditions are not service lists, encryption settings, or user attribute requirements. They are request-context tests evaluated at the time of the API call.

questions.question: An exam question asks which IAM principal type to use for a scenario involving 'a set of humans who all need the same permissions.' What is the answer?

options.text: IAM Role — roles can be shared by multiple users
IAM User — create one user per person and attach policies directly
IAM Group — groups are designed exactly for sets of users with the same permission needs
Root User — the root user can manage permissions for all users

explanation.correct: IAM groups are specifically designed for this use case: attach policies once to the group, add users to the group. All users inherit the group's permissions. When permissions change, update the group — not each user.
explanation.why: Roles are for workloads and temporary access. Direct user attachment is the anti-pattern that groups fix. Root user is for account setup only.

questions.question: Why is the following an anti-pattern: creating dev-user, staging-user, prod-user (one per environment, shared by all team members)?

options.text: It increases AWS costs per environment
It makes IAM harder to configure
It destroys person-level auditability — CloudTrail cannot identify which individual developer took which action
AWS does not allow more than one IAM user per account

explanation.correct: When multiple engineers share a single IAM user, CloudTrail logs show 'dev-user called DeleteObject' but cannot identify WHICH developer did it. This makes incident response impossible. The correct pattern: one IAM identity per human, with environment access controlled through group membership or role assumption.
explanation.why: Shared IAM users have no billing impact and are technically allowed. The problem is purely audit and accountability.

questions.question: An EC2 instance needs to access DynamoDB. Which method is correct?

options.text: Create an IAM user, generate access keys, and set them as environment variables on the instance
Create an IAM user, store access keys in AWS Secrets Manager, and have the instance retrieve them
Create an IAM role with DynamoDB permissions and attach it as an instance profile to the EC2 instance
Use the root user credentials stored in the instance's user data script

explanation.correct: IAM roles via instance profiles are the correct mechanism for giving EC2 instances AWS service access. The role's temporary credentials are automatically rotated and delivered via the instance metadata service. No key management required.
explanation.why: Access keys (A and B) are long-lived and create credential exposure risk even in Secrets Manager. Root credentials (D) have maximum blast radius and are an extreme security violation.

questions.question: A new employee joins the data analytics team. Using a group-based IAM model, what is the ONLY action needed to grant them the team's standard permissions?

options.text: Create a new IAM policy for the employee and attach it to their user
Add the employee's IAM user to the DataAnalystGroup — they inherit all group policies automatically
Copy the policies from another analyst's user to the new employee's user
Create a new IAM role for the employee with the same policies as existing analysts

explanation.correct: In a group-based model, adding a user to the group is the only action needed. The user immediately inherits all policies attached to the group. This is the entire operational benefit of groups.
explanation.why: Creating new policies defeats the purpose of groups. Copying policies is the per-user anti-pattern. Creating new roles for each analyst is unnecessary overhead.

questions.question: What is the IAM evaluation rule for a scenario where an identity-based policy explicitly allows an action AND a bucket policy explicitly denies the same action for the same principal?

options.text: Allow — identity-based policies take precedence over resource-based policies
Allow — when policies conflict, the Allow always wins
Deny — the bucket policy explicit Deny overrides the identity-based Allow (explicit deny wins)
Depends on whether the principal and bucket are in the same AWS account

explanation.correct: Explicit deny wins — always. The bucket policy's explicit Deny overrides the identity-based Allow regardless of account, regardless of which policy was created first, regardless of what other Allows exist. This is the invariant rule.
explanation.why: The account boundary does NOT affect the explicit deny rule. Deny always wins over Allow in all scenarios.

questions.question: A Solutions Architect is designing IAM for a fintech startup. The CISO requires: (1) no long-lived access keys anywhere, (2) all API calls audited, (3) production deletion requires MFA issued within 5 minutes, (4) developers cannot escalate to admin. Which COMBINATION of four AWS features addresses all requirements?

options.text: IAM users with access keys + CloudTrail + MFA at sign-in + AdministratorAccess for developers
IAM roles via instance profiles + CloudTrail data events + aws:MultiFactorAuthAge: 300 + permission boundaries on developer roles
STS temporary credentials + AWS Config + aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent + SCPs
IAM Identity Center + GuardDuty + MFA at sign-in + SCP denying admin

explanation.correct: (1) IAM roles via instance profiles = no long-lived access keys. (2) CloudTrail data events = all API calls audited. (3) aws:MultiFactorAuthAge: 300 (NumericLessThan) = MFA within last 5 minutes for deletion. (4) Permission boundaries on developer roles = cap maximum permissions, no admin escalation.
explanation.why: A uses long-lived access keys (violates requirement 1) and gives developers admin (violates requirement 4). MultiFactorAuthPresent doesn't enforce recency (violates requirement 3). GuardDuty detects but doesn't enforce MFA recency.

questions.question: A bucket policy in Account A grants a role in Account B access to s3:GetObject. The role in Account B does NOT have a policy allowing s3:GetObject on Account A's bucket. Can the role access the bucket?

options.text: Yes — a bucket policy alone is sufficient for same-account and cross-account access
No — cross-account access requires explicit Allow on BOTH sides: source account (role policy) AND destination account (bucket policy)
Yes — the bucket policy in Account A is sufficient since it explicitly grants access to the Account B role
No — bucket policies cannot grant cross-account access; only IAM roles can

explanation.correct: Cross-account access requires explicit Allow on both sides. The bucket policy in Account A is one side (destination). But the role in Account B also needs an identity-based policy allowing s3:GetObject on that specific bucket ARN (source side). Without both Allows, access is denied by implicit deny at the source.
explanation.why: Option A is correct for same-account (bucket policy alone can be sufficient) but not for cross-account. Cross-account tightens the rule to require both sides. Bucket policies CAN grant cross-account access — that's one of their key features — but both sides must allow.
